title: Iran Blacklists 45 Tankers and Approves Hormuz Transit Fees as Rial Crashes Past 2 Million; Rezaei Threatens to Halt All Gulf Oil Exports
subhead: Tehran moved to institutionalize control of the Strait of Hormuz — blacklisting 45 tankers, approving a legal framework for transit fees and threatening to block all Gulf oil exports — just as the US Treasury prepares to unveil its 'greatest financial offensive' against Iran. The rial hit a record low past 2 million to the dollar, and oil held near $93.

sections.heading: Iran Blacklists 45 Tankers, Parliament Approves Hormuz Transit Fees
sections.body:
Iran's state-controlled Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) published a Non-Compliant Vessels list on August 23-24 blacklisting 45 tankers it says violated its transit protocols, threatening fines, detention or cargo confiscation — including crude and LNG — on future passages, according to the New York Post and CNBC. The list includes vessels linked to UAE's ADNOC Logistics and Shipping, its subsidiary Navig8 Tankers, and Saudi national carrier Bahri. Tehran also warned that any ship conducting ship-to-ship transfers with blacklisted hulls faces penalties.

In parallel, Iran's parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission approved Article 3 of the 'Strategic Action Plan for Security and Development of the Strait of Hormuz', creating statutory authority to charge foreign vessels transit and service fees in rials or foreign currency, per Anadolu Agency and Farsi-language reporting cited by Region Alert. The legislation still needs full parliamentary approval.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran is trying to convert military control of the strait into a permanent, revenue-generating administrative regime — a move that would entrench its claim over a waterway carrying roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil, and directly challenge the US naval blockade and Omani-corridor routing.

sections.heading: US Treasury Readies 'Greatest Financial Offensive' as Bessent Declares 'Economic D-Day'
sections.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US will unveil 'the single greatest financial offensive ever' against Iran on Monday, posting on X that 'at dawn begins an economic D-Day' and framing the measures as the 'endgame' of Washington's campaign, per CNBC and the New York Post. The announcement is expected at 1 p.m. ET and will add to an existing sanctions regime targeting Iran's banking, energy, aviation and crypto sectors, with Reuters reporting the Treasury is readying secondary sanctions on entities still doing business with Tehran.

Bessent warned in a Financial Times op-ed that 'any nation that serves as a financial artery of a withering regime should expect to share in its isolation,' language aimed at foreign governments and companies still transacting with Iran — including those purchasing and transporting its petroleum.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the sharpest escalation of the economic-war track of the conflict. By threatening secondary sanctions on third-country buyers and financial intermediaries, Washington is trying to strangle Iran's remaining oil revenue and force a diplomatic settlement — while Tehran has vowed to treat any nation joining the measures as an enemy.

sections.heading: Rial Crashes Past 2 Million to the Dollar as Economic Strain Mounts
sections.body:
The Iranian rial hit a record open-market low, with the dollar surpassing 2 million rials for the first time in history, according to Gulf News and Farsi independent media cited by CNBC and Region Alert. The collapse comes as markets price in the new US sanctions round and as the war enters its sixth month.

Even senior Iranian officials are publicly acknowledging the strain. President Masoud Pezeshkian said 'the war must come to an end at some point,' and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned that 'no matter how much military power we have, if people are hungry and we do not have financial circulation and economic growth, we will not endure,' per the New York Post citing Iranian state media.
sections.whyItMatters: The currency collapse is the clearest evidence yet that the economic-war track is biting. Tehran's own leadership is signaling war fatigue, which may be the opening Washington is betting on — but it also raises the risk of a desperate military response as the regime's room to maneuver narrows.

sections.heading: Rezaei Threatens to Block All Gulf Oil Exports if US Pressure Continues
sections.body:
Iran's new Supreme National Security Council secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, vowed on August 23 to halt all regional oil exports from the Persian Gulf if US economic pressure continues, declaring that any foreign participation in US sanctions would be treated as an 'act of war,' per CNBC and Region Alert citing Iranian state media. He also threatened to target the interests of oil-rich neighbors that join US efforts to isolate Iran.

The threat comes as the US Navy's maritime coalition — more than 20 warships including destroyers USS John Finn and USS Ross — has redirected 70 commercial vessels, disabled three and seized two since mid-July, per CENTCOM figures cited by Region Alert.
sections.whyItMatters: Rezaei's threat to cut off the entire Gulf's exports — not just Iran's own — is a qualitative escalation of the chokepoint standoff. If acted on, it would hit Saudi, UAE and Kuwaiti barrels, not just Iranian ones, and would test whether the US naval escort operation can actually keep ~20 million barrels a day moving.

sections.heading: Who Controls Hormuz? Shipping Data Shows a Fractured, Dark-Routing Waterway
sections.body:
Maritime intelligence firm Kpler data shows 112 oil and gas tankers transited the Strait of Hormuz between August 1 and 19 — versus roughly 130 ships a day before the war. Of those, 21 openly used the Iranian route, only two the Omani route, and 89 (over 80%) went 'dark' with AIS transponders off or on unclassified routes, per Al Jazeera's analysis. When all cargo vessels are included, 35% openly used the Iranian route.

Analysts draw opposite conclusions from the same data. Al Jazeera's experts (Chatham House's Neil Quilliam, researcher Marc Ayoub) say the fear of offending Tehran still outweighs Trump's threats, with Iran retaining significant capacity to disrupt traffic. Gulf News and CNN, by contrast, argue Iran has 'at least partially lost control' as more vessels hug the Omani corridor under US escort, with Energy Secretary Chris Wright citing combined transits of around 15 million barrels a day in a recent week.
sections.whyItMatters: The 'dark routing' — ships switching off transponders to avoid targeting — makes it impossible to verify either side's control claims. The practical reality is a heavily throttled, militarized waterway where both Iran and the US can raise costs but neither fully dictates terms, keeping a security premium baked into oil prices.

sections.heading: Iraqi Tankers Get Passage, Pakistan's Army Chief Mediates in Tehran
sections.body:
Iran granted permission for a number of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz following repeated requests from Baghdad, Reuters reported on August 22 — a sign Tehran is selectively easing its own blockade for friendly neighbors even as it tightens rules for others.

Separately, Pakistan's Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir traveled to Tehran on August 24 to lead high-level mediation between Iran and regional states, per Region Alert, as Islamabad seeks to protect its refined-product imports and LNG shipments from Gulf disruption. Pakistan is managing domestic fuel rationing and elevated petroleum levies amid the shipping crisis.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran is weaponizing passage permission as a diplomatic tool — rewarding Iraq while threatening others — and Pakistan's military-led mediation shows how deeply the Hormuz crisis is now pulling in non-Gulf Asian states that depend on the waterway for fuel and LNG.

sections.heading: Alternative Routes: BTC Holds, South Korea Tests the Arctic Northern Sea Route
sections.body:
With Hormuz throttled, alternative corridors are absorbing pressure. The Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline is operating at normal throughput, moving 14.77 million tons of crude from January through July, with BP's 11-day maintenance on the Central Azeri platform not disrupting export commitments, per Region Alert. Azeri Light crude is trading firm near $96 a barrel on European refiner demand for non-Gulf barrels.

In a notable test of long-term alternatives, the South Korean container ship PanStar Acro departed Busan on August 22 on a 45-day trial voyage to Europe via the Arctic Northern Sea Route, per Region Alert — an attempt to find a route around disrupted Middle Eastern waterways.
sections.whyItMatters: The BTC corridor and Caspian barrels are quietly becoming more valuable as Gulf seaborne exports are constrained, and the Arctic trial signals that prolonged Hormuz disruption is pushing even Asian shippers to explore routes that were previously uneconomic — a shift with long-term implications for trade geography.

bottomLine: The US-Iran economic war escalated sharply on both sides: Washington is rolling out its 'greatest financial offensive' with expanded secondary sanctions, while Tehran blacklisted 45 tankers, approved a legal framework for Hormuz transit fees, and saw its currency crash past 2 million rials to the dollar. Iran's own leadership is publicly signaling war fatigue, but Rezaei's threat to cut off all Gulf oil exports raises the stakes for the entire region. Oil held near $93 as markets weigh a throttled, dark-routing Hormuz against the possibility that economic pressure finally forces a settlement. The next 48 hours — the sanctions rollout and Omani FM's Tuesday visit to Tehran — will show whether this is the endgame or another escalation cycle.
sources: CNBC, New York Post, Reuters, Al Jazeera, Gulf News, Anadolu Agency, Region Alert, Kpler, Chatham House, Financial Times, CENTCOM
